MUQATIL:18:45-46/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:45-46/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:45-46/r1.claim: The rain-and-plant parable warns Meccan unbelievers that worldly life withers and perishes when the Hereafter comes; God can resurrect.

MUQATIL:18:45-46/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:18:45-46/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:18:45-46/r2.claim: The parable shows that God has power over everything, including resurrection.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p188/r8.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p188/r8.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p188/r8.claim: The worldly life is like plants that flourish after rain and then are shredded and scattered by winds: worldly beauty soon disappears, while God can do all things.

FARRA:v2p145/r7.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p145/r7.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p145/r7.claim: تذروه is a variant of تذريه; Abdullah reads تذريه الريح, and a reading from أذريت would mean to cast or scatter it, as in al-Mufaddal's poem.

MAJAZ:v1p404/r7.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p404/r7.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p404/r7.claim: Tadhruhu al-riyāḥ means the wind scatters it; dharathu/dharūhu and adhartha/tudhrīhi are alternate forms.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p268#3/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p268#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p268#3/r1.claim: Tadhruhu al-riyāḥ means the winds scatter it.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p268#3/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p268#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p268#3/r2.claim: Muqtadir is formed on the iftaʿala pattern from qadara.

TAB-FULL:v15p272/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p272/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p272/r1.claim: The worldly-life parable addresses arrogant people who asked that the believers devoted to God be expelled: worldly life is like rain-fed growth that soon dries and scatters.

TAB-FULL:v15p272/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p272/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p272/r2.claim: The plant becomes dry fragments scattered by winds; ذرو describes scattering, with several Arabic verb forms for blowing something away.

TAB-FULL:v15p272/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p272/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p272/r3.claim: An unnamed poet’s line using يذرك illustrates the sense of casting or blowing someone off a mount.

TAB-FULL:v15p272/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v15p272/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v15p272/r4.claim: God can ruin gardens and worldly wealth; people should not boast or grow arrogant over wealth, since worldly life fades, while they should work for the enduring afterlife.

ZAJJAJ:v3p290/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p290/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p290/r3.claim: The rain nourishes vegetation until it dries into wind-scattered chaff; الرياح is read, and two other forms of تذروه are possible but not recited.

ZAJJAJ:v3p290/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p290/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p290/r4.claim: The example teaches that worldly life passes away, and what has passed is as though it never existed.

ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r1.claim: God has power to originate and annihilate all things.

ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r2.speaker: الحسن
ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r2.claim: Al-Hasan says God was able to bring each thing into being before its creation.

ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r3.speaker: سيبويه والخليل
ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r3.claim: Sibawayh and al-Khalil's view is preferred: كَان describes timeless power; Arabic does not use past كَان for future or present without a tense-shifting particle.

ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p291/r4.claim: Some say God's كان means كائن ويكون, but this conflicts with normal Arabic tense usage.

NAHHAS:v2p458/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p458/r13.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v2p458/r13.claim: He also allows ʿuqbā on the pattern of bushrā.

NAHHAS:v2p458/r14.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p458/r14.speaker: القراء العامة
NAHHAS:v2p458/r14.claim: The common reading is tadhruhu; ʿAbd Allāh’s reading and another report from al-Kisāʾī have tadh rīhi.

NAHHAS:v2p458/r15.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p458/r15.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v2p458/r15.claim: He explains adhraytu a man from a camel as turning or rolling him over.

NAHHAS:v2p459/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p459/r1.speaker: قوم
NAHHAS:v2p459/r1.claim: Some say kāna means ‘will be’; others say it means ‘has always been.’

NAHHAS:v2p459/r14.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p459/r14.speaker: سيبويه والمفضل
NAHHAS:v2p459/r14.claim: They cite an anonymous line containing tazlaq as poetic evidence for the verb’s usage.

NAHHAS:v2p459/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p459/r2.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v2p459/r2.claim: He rejects using a past-tense form for the future unless a contextual particle signals it.

NAHHAS:v2p459/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p459/r3.speaker: سيبويه
NAHHAS:v2p459/r3.claim: The best explanation is that people witnessed God’s power and were told He has always been powerful.

SULAMI:v1p411#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p411#3/r1.speaker: محمد بن الفضل
SULAMI:v1p411#3/r1.claim: The world is the lower self's close companion, to which it continually inclines; its inward and outward adornments draw people toward it.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p172#2/r1.claim: The parable addresses the arrogant wealthy people who asked Muhammad to dismiss poor believers.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p172#2/r10.claim: He glosses تذروه as turning or moving it around.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r11.speaker: ابن كيسان
THALABI:v6p172#2/r11.claim: He explains the winds as bringing the plants back and forth.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r12.speaker: الأخفش
THALABI:v6p172#2/r12.claim: He glosses تذروه as raising the plant.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r13.speaker: أبو عبيدة
THALABI:v6p172#2/r13.claim: He says the winds scatter the plant.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r14.speaker: القتيبي
THALABI:v6p172#2/r14.claim: He glosses the verb as blowing the plant away.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r15.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r15.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
THALABI:v6p172#2/r15.claim: His reading gives forms meaning the wind scattered or lifted the plant away.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p172#2/r2.claim: The water in the parable is rain.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r3.speaker: الحكماء
THALABI:v6p172#2/r3.claim: They compare worldly life to water because neither stays in one place or remains in one condition.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r4.speaker: الحكماء
THALABI:v6p172#2/r4.claim: Water eventually disappears, as worldly life also comes to an end.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r5.speaker: الحكماء
THALABI:v6p172#2/r5.claim: No one can enter water without getting wet, just as no one escapes the trials and harms of worldly life.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r6.speaker: الحكماء
THALABI:v6p172#2/r6.claim: Water in its proper measure is useful, while excess is destructive; sufficient worldly provision helps, but surplus harms.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v6p172#2/r7.claim: He glosses هشيم as dried up.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r8.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v6p172#2/r8.claim: He glosses هشيم as broken or crushed.

THALABI:v6p172#2/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p172#2/r9.speaker: الأخفش
THALABI:v6p172#2/r9.claim: He says هشيم means crumbled, from a root meaning breaking.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r1.claim: Water may have mixed with plants as they matured.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r2.claim: Alternatively, plants mixed together and grew after the water fell.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r3.claim: Hāshīm is plant matter crumbled after drying; water's absence is implicit for concision.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r4.speaker: الشاعر
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r4.claim: A poem likens dead bodies to dried plant matter, illustrating hāshīm.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r5.claim: One purpose is to show the world's beauty and delight passing away.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p309/r6.claim: Alternatively, adversity accompanies every blessing and sorrow every joy.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r1.claim: The example is addressed to the Prophet's people.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r2.claim: The comparison “like water” is a predicate of an omitted subject: worldly life is like water.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r3.claim: The water sent down from heaven is rain.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r4.claim: “It mingled” means the vegetation entwined and gathered because of the water, since water makes plants grow abundantly.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r5.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r5.claim: Abu Ishaq says the water penetrates the plants until they become lush; the plant is mixed with the water by being watered.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r6.claim: The plant becomes hasheem: brittle, broken vegetation; the word derives from breaking, as in breaking bread, and is related to the name Hashim.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r7.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p33#2/r7.claim: Exegetes describe hasheem as broken and crumbled vegetation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r1.claim: “The winds scatter it” means wind carries an object, raises it, and stirs it; the verb has several dialect forms, and Ibn Masud reads “tudhrihi.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r2.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r2.claim: The phrase means the winds lift, disperse, and blow the vegetation away.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r3.claim: This image is a shortened version of the water-and-vegetation example in Yunus, which al-Wahidi explains there in detail.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r4.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God teaches that worldly life passes away, using this comparison.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r5.claim: God is capable of creating and ending everything: He brought vegetation into existence and then made it perish.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r6.speaker: الحسن
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r6.claim: Hasan says God was able to bring every thing into being before it existed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r7.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p34/r7.claim: Al-Zajjaj says grammarians understand “was able” as “has always been able”; the power people witness is not newly acquired by God.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:45-46/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:45-46/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:45-46/r1.claim: Worldly life is like rain that makes the earth's plants grow lush before they crumble into fragments carried away by the wind.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:45-46/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:45-46/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:18:45-46/r2.claim: This is a shortened version of the parable in 10:24; God can create plants from nothing and then destroy them.

JISHUMI:v6p4423/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4423/r10.speaker: الأصم
JISHUMI:v6p4423/r10.claim: Al-Asamm interprets the rain as mixing with the vegetation.

JISHUMI:v6p4423/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4423/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4423/r5.claim: Hashim describes hollow things broken apart, especially dried and crumbled plants; tadhriya is the wind scattering light things in every direction.

JISHUMI:v6p4423/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4423/r7.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
JISHUMI:v6p4423/r7.claim: Talha b. Musarrif reads تذريه instead of the common تذروه; both forms are dialectal variants.

JISHUMI:v6p4423/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4423/r9.speaker: الأصم
JISHUMI:v6p4423/r9.claim: The command to give the worldly life as a parable is attached to what precedes and addresses arrogant people who prefer the passing world; the addressees are also variously identified as those denying its end or the people of Mecca, as al-Asamm relates.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r1.claim: Rain brings out plants of every color and flower, but soon they dry into brittle fragments that the wind carries away.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r2.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r2.claim: They gloss hasīman as something broken and crumbled.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r3.claim: He glosses tadharūhu as the wind stirring it up.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r4.claim: He glosses it as scattering it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r5.speaker: القتيبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p174/r5.claim: He glosses it as blowing it away.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r1.claim: The water causes earthly plants to intertwine and grow dense.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r2.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r2.claim: Another explanation is that water permeates the vegetation, mixing with it until it is lush; the wording is sound because each of two mixed things can take the other’s quality.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r3.claim: Hashim is vegetation broken and crushed; its singular is hashimah.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r4.claim: A reading has “the wind scatters it”; Ibn Abbas reads “the winds scatter it,” using the causative form.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r5.claim: The worldly life’s freshness and beauty followed by ruin is like lush green growth that withers and blows away as if it never existed.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p677/r6.claim: God has power over all things in bringing them into being and making them perish.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r1.claim: The worldly life in the parable means human life together with its blessings and comforts; the comparison says that it is like water.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r2.claim: The vegetation mixed together because of the water; the bāʾ indicates cause, and aṣbaḥa means became rather than specifically morning.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r3.speaker: الربيع بن ضبع
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r3.claim: Rabīʿ b. Dabʿ's line shows aṣbaḥa used for a resulting state rather than a time of morning.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r4.claim: Hasheem is brittle, fragmented dry vegetation; the word also underlies breaking up tharid, and tadhru means scatter.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas reads tadhrihi, meaning that the winds pull the vegetation up and cast it away; al-Hasan and others read wind in the singular.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r6.speaker: سيبويه
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r6.claim: Sibawayh takes kāna as conveying that this was already the case before humans existed, something reason recognizes.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r7.speaker: الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r7.claim: Al-Hasan reads kāna as reporting the state before created things existed: God's power already was.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p519#2/r8.claim: The flourishing plant mirrors worldly beauty, power, and pride that fade, while a person's righteous work remains in the afterlife.

RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r1.claim: This is another parable showing the world's insignificance and short duration, aimed at wealthy polytheists who boast of riches and supporters over poor believers.

RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r2.claim: Rain makes the earth's plants grow, sway, and look beautiful, as another verse says that the earth stirs and swells after rain.

RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r3.claim: After a time the vegetation dries into hashim, broken and crumbled plant matter, then winds scatter it in every direction.

RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r4.claim: An unnamed poem uses هشّم for crushing bread, illustrating the sense of breaking or crumbling.

RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r5.claim: God's power appears in bringing the plant into being, nurturing it, and then abolishing it; worldly life likewise grows from beauty to decline and extinction.

RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r6.claim: Because worldly beauty inevitably declines into destruction, a rational person should not take delight in it.

RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r7.claim: One grammatical explanation of باء in فاختلط به نبات الأرض is that kinds of plants mix with one another because rain strengthens and entangles them.

RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v21p111/r8.claim: A second explanation is that water mixes with plants and plants with water until they are saturated and lush; either mingled thing may take the other's description.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r1.claim: Hashīm is dry, broken, crumbling vegetation after water stops; the root also describes dry wood, a generous person, a weak body, showing affection, milking a camel, and crumbling bread.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبعرى
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r2.claim: Ibn al-Zibara’s verse praises Amr al-Ula for crumbling bread to feed Mecca’s lean, famine-struck people; Hashim’s name came from breaking and serving the bread after a famine.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r3.claim: The author recounts how Hashim brought bread and camels from Syria, crumbled the bread into pots, and fed Mecca during years of hardship, earning the name Hashim.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن قتيبة وابن كيسان وابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r4.claim: They gloss tadhruhu as dispersing, scattering, carrying to and fro, or turning about; the author says the senses are close.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r5.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف وابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r5.claim: Talha reads tadhrihi al-riḥ, and the codex of Ibn Masud likewise has tadhrihi; forms of the verb mean that wind carries something off.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r6.speaker: سيبويه والفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#2/r6.claim: A line cited by Sibawayh and al-Farra uses the verb for wind blowing a bird off course, illustrating the sense of scattering.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#3/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45#3/r1.claim: God is fully able to originate, annihilate, and bring things to life.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r1.claim: The water-and-plant example is directed at the arrogant leaders who asked that poor believers be expelled; the earth’s plants grow lush after rain and then fade.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r2.claim: The plant may be said to mix through the water until flourishing, or to mix with one another after rain, since rain makes vegetation abundant.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r3.speaker: الحكماء
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r3.claim: The sages compare worldly life with water because neither stays fixed, water vanishes as life does, and no one enters worldly life without exposure to its trials and harms.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r4.speaker: الحكماء
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r4.claim: Water in the right measure benefits, while excess destroys; likewise enough of worldly goods helps and surplus harms.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r5.claim: A man asking to be among the successful is told to leave worldly life and take from it like still water: little suffices and much intoxicates.

QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:18:45/r6.claim: Muslim reports the Prophet saying successful is the one who submits, receives enough, and is made content with what God gives.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r1.claim: The parable recalls worldly life in its beauty and rapid disappearance, or its extraordinary quality; water may be a predicate or a second object of make.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r2.claim: Plants intermingle through dense growth or absorb water until refreshed; reversing the usual phrasing intensifies the image of abundance.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r3.claim: The image is the full progression: lush growth nourished by rain becomes broken debris scattered by winds, as if it never existed.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r4.claim: Tadhruhu means scatter it; another reading uses tadhrihi from a different verb.

BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:18:45/r5.claim: Hishim means crushed and broken; God's power encompasses both bringing things into being and making them perish.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p16/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p16/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p16/r1.claim: The water makes the plants mingle and thicken together, or the water itself enters and saturates the plants.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p16/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p16/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p16/r2.claim: Hashīm is dry, broken vegetation; tadhruhu means the wind scatters and blows it away, with a plural-wind reading by Ḥamza and ʿĀṣim.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p16/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p16/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p16/r3.claim: The world's fresh beauty followed by ruin is like green plants that dry and are blown away as if they had never existed; God can create and annihilate.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r1.speaker: الفراء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r1.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains hashīm as dry plant matter and gives hashīma as its singular.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r2.speaker: الزجاج وابن قتيبة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r2.claim: Al-Zajjāj and Ibn Qutayba define hashīm as something once moist that has dried, like brittle fodder or crumbled bread; its root sense is dry vegetation broken apart.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r3.speaker: أبو عبيدة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r3.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says dharā and adh­rā are two forms meaning to scatter.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r4.speaker: ابن كيسان
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p183/r4.claim: Ibn Kaysān says tadhruhu means the wind carries it here and there.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r1.speaker: الأخفش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r1.claim: Al-Akhfash glosses the wind's action as lifting the plant debris.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r12.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r12.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes the comparison with water as the predicate of an omitted subject, namely that worldly life is like water.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r13.speaker: الحوفي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r13.claim: Al-Ḥawfī attaches the kāf to an implied verbal noun, meaning a striking of a likeness like water.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r14.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r14.claim: Abū Ḥayyān instead parses kamāʾ as the second object of aḍrib: make the likeness of worldly life into something resembling water.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r15.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p184/r15.claim: The author refers to his earlier explanation of the parallel water parable in Sūrat Yūnus.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r1.claim: أصبح هشيما may mean it became dry by morning, since most calamities strike in the morning, or simply became without a time reference; poetry supports the latter.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r2.speaker: الزجاج وابن قتيبة
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r2.claim: They define هشيم as what was moist and then dried; it is the singular of هشيمة, meaning dry vegetation, and the root also describes crumbling bread.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r3.claim: تذروه is an adjective of هشيم; الذرو means scattering, and some gloss it as lifting.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r4.claim: Abdullah reads تذريه, using the alternate yāʾ root for a final radical that varies between wāw and yāʾ.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas reads تذريه with ḍamma on tā, from الإذراء, which may derive from either root.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r6.speaker: زيد بن علي والحسن والنخعي
SAMIN-DURR:18:45#2/r6.claim: Most readers use plural الرياح, while Zayd ibn Ali, al-Hasan, al-Nakhai, and others read singular الريح.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r1.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r1.claim: Ibn Atiyya makes كماء the predicate of an omitted subject, namely the life of this world.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r2.speaker: الحوفي
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r2.claim: Al-Hawfi attaches كماء to an implied verbal noun, ضربا, assuming اضرب is transitive to one object.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r3.claim: The preferred parse makes كماء the second object of اضرب because اضرب here means صير; al-Baqa had already proposed this.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r4.claim: أنزلناه is an adjective describing ماء.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r5.claim: The ب in فاختلط به may express cause or mark transitivity; al-Zamakhshari says the plants thickened and intermixed because of the water.

SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:18:45/r6.claim: Another explanation is that water permeated and refreshed the plants; بنبات الأرض would be expected, but the wording is valid because each of two mixed things takes the other's description.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p161/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p161/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p161/r1.claim: Worldly life fades like rain-fed vegetation: it grows and becomes beautiful, then dries into fragments scattered in every direction by the wind; God has power over both states and everything else.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p161/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p161/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p161/r2.claim: The same fleeting-life image appears in the parables of 10:24, 39:21, and 57:20; an authentic hadith also calls the world sweet and green.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r1.claim: Worldly life for everyone resembles rain-fed vegetation: it becomes lush and varied, then withers, breaks apart, and is scattered, exposing the world’s brief allure.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r2.claim: Rain descends from above by God’s power and at the needed time; the water mingles with soil and produces varied, dense growth that God later dries.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r3.claim: “Withered debris” means dry, crumbled vegetation; the winds stir it, scatter it, and carry it away.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r4.claim: God’s power to create, destroy, and restore is eternal, not newly acquired.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p471/r5.claim: Like a crop, worldly life first flourishes and increases, then declines into extinction; its toil and anxieties make it unworthy of pride and a reason to seek lasting bliss.

BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r1.claim: The brother's admonition failed because the listener's heart had become harder, so his outcome was regret.

BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r2.claim: The worldly-life parable should show its beauty, freshness, and swift disappearance so people do not rely on it or abandon the afterlife.

BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r3.claim: The comparison is explained as the world being like water; heaven here can mean a cloud or the direction of the sky.

BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p192#2/r4.claim: The comparison concerns the whole sequence within the simile, not water by itself.

BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r1.claim: God has complete power over creating, preserving, and annihilating everything.

BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r2.claim: A rational person should not be deceived by worldly life: it perishes even when long-lasting and vanishes despite its adornment.

BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r3.speaker: الشيخ سعدي
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r3.claim: Saadi's examples of aging, a king's silk shroud eaten by worms, and renewed spring warn that life passes while the world continues.

BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r4.claim: In an inward allegory, primordial care joins spirit to body as water joins earth; prophets and saints sow faith and monotheism through invitation in the heart's fertile soil, nourished by the Law.

BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r5.claim: The seed of monotheism grows into faith, raising the spirit from low human nature toward spiritual ranks and divine nearness through the good word and righteous action.

BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r6.claim: God may abandon the spirit to animal-like corporeality or draw it by grace to the highest nearness, where even the angels prostrate to it.

BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r7.speaker: المولى الجامي
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r7.claim: Jami says seekers cannot arrive through years of effort alone without the beloved's attraction.

BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r8.speaker: وهب
BURSEVI:v5p193#2/r8.claim: Wahb says an account in a book calls worldly life a gain for the discerning and heedlessness for the ignorant; prophets and saints lived in it without attachment.

BURSEVI:v5p193/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p193/r1.claim: The earth's plants intertwine and grow dense from the water, making the land fresh and flourishing.

BURSEVI:v5p193/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p193/r2.claim: هشيما means the vegetation has become dry, crushed, and broken; the root refers to breaking something soft.

BURSEVI:v5p193/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p193/r3.claim: The winds carry the broken plants away and scatter them; the lexicon also uses the verb for winnowing grain in wind.

BURSEVI:v5p193/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p193/r4.claim: This verse condenses the fuller parable of worldly life in Yunus.

BURSEVI:v5p193/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p193/r5.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v5p193/r5.claim: Kashifi compares human youth and freshness to a flourishing tree that death dries out, while hopes and desires are blown into nothingness.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r1.claim: The parable recalls the world’s beauty and rapid disappearance so listeners will not be deceived by it or turn away from the afterlife.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r10.speaker: أبو عبيدة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r10.claim: Abu ʿUbayda says تذروه means “scatter it.”

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r11.speaker: الأخفش
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r11.claim: Al-Akhfash says the wind lifts the debris.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r12.speaker: ابن كيسان
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r12.claim: Ibn Kaysan says the wind brings it and takes it away.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r13.speaker: ابن مسعود
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r13.claim: Ibn Masʿud reads تذريه, a four-form variant of the same verb.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r14.speaker: زيد بن علي والحسن والنخعي والأعمش وطلحة وابن أبي ليلى وابن محيصن وخلف وابن عيسى وابن جرير
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r14.claim: These readers use the singular الريح instead of plural الرياح.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r15.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r15.claim: The comparison is not water alone but the whole scene: water-grown plants flourish, dry, and are scattered until they seem never to have existed.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r16.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r16.claim: The فاء signals how rapidly the vegetation vanishes; another reading treats it as an explanatory فاء with an omitted period of flourishing.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r17.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r17.claim: God has complete power over all things, including bringing creation into being and making it perish.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r2.claim: Alternatively, the command asks the Prophet to explain the world’s remarkable condition, itself like a strange parable.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r3.claim: كماء begins a fresh explanation of the analogy, “it is like water”; construing it as the second object of ضرب is grammatically awkward.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r4.speaker: الحوفي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r4.claim: Al-Hawfi makes the comparison an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning “a striking like water”; the author rejects this analysis.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r5.claim: The plants mingle densely because water is plentiful, or the water enters the plants and makes them full and lush.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r6.claim: Although ordinary usage would say water mingled with the plants, the verse reverses the relation to emphasize water’s abundance, as though it were the primary mass.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r7.claim: هشيما means dry, fragmented vegetation, either an intensive passive form or a plural of هشيمة; أصبح may simply mean “became.”

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r8.claim: Some take أصبح literally as morning, since heavenly calamities often arrive at night; the author says the verse only describes eventual drying.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p285#2/r9.claim: The cycle resembles 87:4–5, where God brings out pasture and makes it dark, dry debris.

ELMALILI:18:45-53/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:45-53/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:45-53/r1.claim: Worldly life is likened to rain that mixes with the earth's plants, then becomes scraps scattered by winds; God has power over everything.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r1.claim: The plants’ intermingling means abundant growth with its parts entwined through fertility and flourishing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r2.claim: The bāʾ is causal and its pronoun refers to water: plants mingle because of the water; it does not make ikhtalaṭ transitive.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r3.claim: Mentioning earth after sky creates antithesis.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r4.claim: Aṣbaḥa is used commonly to mean became.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r5.claim: Hashīm follows faʿīl with passive meaning, crushed or shattered; hashm means breaking and fragmenting.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r6.claim: Tadhruhu al-riyāḥ means winds scatter it through the air; dharw is throwing into the air.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r7.claim: The first simile compares worldly life to a garden whose beauty lasts, then declines; its shared feature is a turn from good to bad, an abstract condition pictured sensorially.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r8.claim: A second composite simile maps prosperity, youth, novelty, and adornment followed by contraction and scattered loss onto rain, abundant growth, decline, and windblown remnants.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p331/r9.claim: The closing clause is parenthetical: God’s power creates things and their opposites and orders causes of decay after causes of persistence; the universal wording serves as a conclusion.

TABATABAI:18:45-46/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:45-46/r1.speaker: الراغب
TABATABAI:18:45-46/r1.claim: The second parable depicts worldly life’s quickly vanishing beauty; hashīm is fragile vegetation broken to pieces, and dharw means scattering, though one gloss says bringing it and taking it away.

TABATABAI:18:45-46/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:45-46/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:45-46/r2.claim: Rain makes the earth’s plants fresh and beautiful, then they become broken fragments scattered by winds, illustrating how worldly adornment quickly vanishes.

TABATABAI:18:45-46/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:45-46/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:45-46/r3.claim: Saying the rain “mixed with it” emphasizes water’s role in forming vegetation; rain is named because other water sources begin with it, and “became” does not restrict the change to morning.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The next parable addresses people blinded by love of worldly life: its ornaments will not accompany them to the next world; only righteous deeds endure as what they can earn.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Worldly allure blinds the affluent as they become entangled in material pursuits.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Al-Ḥadīd explains the parable as worldly amusement, adornment, and competition in wealth and children; its luxuriant growth lures disbelievers before withering.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The affluent are so captivated by luxury, possessions, status, and comfort that they make no time for anything else.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Worldly luxuriance is temporary: rain first creates it, but it soon withers, and God has power both to produce and to decay it.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:45/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:45/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:45/r1.claim: Some wealthy Meccans, proud of property and sons, rejected monotheism and claimed life was only worldly; the verse compares transient worldly life to flourishing vegetation that soon dries and scatters.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:45/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:45/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:45/r2.claim: Worldly life is fleeting and wealth and children are its adornment; these pass away, while righteous deeds endure.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:45/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:45/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:45/r5.claim: Islam disapproves of using blessings as grounds for arrogance toward the poor or as material and psychological pressure.

QIRAAT-ER:18:45:22#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:45:22#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:45:22#1/r1.claim: The singular rīḥ reading contrasts with plural riyāḥ and is associated in classical usage with destructive wind.

STUDYQURAN:18:45/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:45/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:45/r1.claim: This parable restates the lesson of verses 32–44: worldly life depends on divine beneficence, flourishes through God’s power and mercy, then becomes lifeless chaff.

STUDYQURAN:18:45/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:45/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:45/r2.claim: The chaff image recalls the disbeliever’s flourishing gardens ending as a barren plain and resembles other Quranic parables.
